abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) includes a defining hallmark that correlates most closely to cognitive decline, namely misfolded tau protein. However, the “upstream” etiology and downstream clinical manifestations of tauopathies are quite diverse. Tau deposition elicits different pathological phenotypes and outcomes depending on the tau strain, proteoforms, and regional susceptibility. Posttranslational modifications (PTM) can alter tau structure, function, networks, and its pathological sequelae. We uncovered tau citrullination on multiple epitopes caused by peptidyl arginine deiminase (PAD) enzymes. PAD-induced citrullination irreversibly converts arginine residues to citrulline, producing a net loss of positive charge, elimination of pi–pi interactions, and increased hydrophobicity. We observed increased PAD2 and PAD4 in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) brain and that they both can citrullinate tau. Tau can become citrullinated by PADs at all 14 arginine residues throughout the N-terminal domain (N-term), proline-rich domain (PR), microtubule-binding repeats domain (MBR), and C-terminal domain (C-term) on full-length tau (2N4R). Citrullination of tau impacts fibrillization and oligomerization rates in aggregation assays. Utilizing a panel of novel citrullinated tau (citR tau) antibodies, we identified citrullination of tau in vitro, several animal models of tauopathies, and Alzheimer’s disease (AD). CitR tau increased with Braak stage and was enriched in AD brains with higher pathological tau burden. This work provides a new area of tau biology that signifies further consideration in the emerging spectrum of tauopathies and its clinical understanding. Recombinant tau, construct cloning, protein purification, and
in vitro
citrullination
Recombinant human 2N4R (441 tau protein) was purchased from (cat#T1001, rPeptide, GA, USA). For in vitro citrullination, 2 μg (1 μg/μl) of recombinant tau was incubated with 2 µg (1 μg/μl) or decreasing concentrations of peptidyl arginine deaminases (PAD2 or PAD4, MI, USA) (Cayman, MI, USA) in PAD reaction buffer (50 mM boric acid, 2–10 mM CaCl2 dihydrous, pH 8.0, Cayman, 10,500, GA, USA) (Cayman, MI, USA) at 37 °C for 60–90 min.
Tau 0N4R gene variants, including wild type, P301L, R349Q and All R → Q, were synthesized by Twist Bioscience and cloned in the pET28a (+) vector between the BamH1 and HindIII sites. In addition, a TEV cleavage site was added to the N-terminal of all genes.
Tau variant 0N4R with His-tag and tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease TEV-tag located at the N-terminal was cloned in pET28a + vector and expressed in
E. coli
of BL21 DE3 cells (New England Biolabs, Cat# C2527H). Tau proteins were induced in 1 L lysogeny broth (LB) by adding 1 mM isopropyl β- d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) at the density OD600 = 0.7–0.8 for 3 h at 37 degrees. Cells were harvested, and pellets were resuspended in binding/wash buffer (20 mM Tris, 500 mM NaCl, 15 mM imidazole, pH 8.0) with proteinase inhibitors, followed by sonication at 85% power, 10″ on, 10″ off for 5 min (Fisher Brand Sonicator, FB120/CL-18) and centrifugation at 30,000 g for 30 min at 4 °C. The soluble (supernatant) fraction was passed through a 2 mL Ni–NTA column (G-Biosciences, Cat# 786-940), followed by washing with binding/wash buffer, and the protein was subsequently eluted with buffer containing 20 mM Tris, 500 mM NaCl, 300 mM imidazole, and pH 8.0. TEV cleavage was performed by dialysis against TEV buffer (50 mM Tris HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl) in the presence of TEV protease (GenScript Cat#Z03030) at room temperature for 4 h. The TEV proteinase-cleaved tau was re-purified by reverse-Ni–NTA column. Briefly, the column was equilibrated with binding/wash buffer and the cleaved protein was collected in the flow-through solution. Cleaved tau was further purified by a FPLC system (The ӒKTA pure™
chromatography
system from
Cytiva
™) at 4 °C using a HiLoad16/600 Superdex200pg column in SEC buffer (20 mM Tris, 500 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM DTT, pH 7.6).
Mass spectroscopy
Samples from enzyme reactions with tau protein incubated with PAD2 or PAD4 were separated by SDS-PAGE and Coomassie-stained for visualization. Bands were excised from the gel and processed for LC–MS/MS analysis. Briefly, each gel piece was minced and de-stained before being reduced with dithiothreitol (DTT), alkylated with iodoacetamide (IAA), and finally digested with Trypsin/Lys-C overnight at 37 °C. Peptides were extracted using 50/50 acetonitrile (ACN)/H
2
O/0.1% formic acid and dried in a vacuum concentrator. Peptides were resuspended in 98% H
2
O/2% ACN/0.1% formic acid for LC–MS/MS analysis.
Peptides were separated on a 50 cm C18 reversed-phase UHPLC column (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) using an Ultimate3000 UHPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) with a 60 min gradient (4–40% ACN/0.1% formic acid) and analyzed on a hybrid quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Q Exactive Plus, Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) using data-dependent acquisition in which the top 10 most abundant ions are selected for MS/MS analysis. Full MS survey scans were acquired at 70,000 resolution.
Raw data files were processed in MaxQuant (
www.maxquant.org
) and searched against the current Uniprot
Homo sapiens
protein sequence database. Search parameters included constant modification of cysteine by carbamidomethylation, and the variable modifications, methionine oxidation, arginine citrullination, as well as asparagine and glutamine deamidation. Proteins are identified using the filtering criteria of 1% protein and peptide false discovery rate, with a peptide tolerance of 4.5 ppm.
To ensure the correct identification of the site-specific citrullination of Tau411, several factors were taken into consideration. MS/MS spectra were manually annotated to verify the sequence coverage of each citrulline-containing peptide. The verification process further included consideration of deamidation of asparagine and glutamine, which results in an identical mass shift as the citrullination of arginine. While deamidation cannot be differentiated from citrullination based on mass, deamidation does not affect the charge of the amino acid residue (under acidic LC–MS conditions); however, citrulline neutralizes a positively charged arginine. The reduced positive charge/increased hydrophobicity of a peptide containing a citrullinated arginine results in a later elution time compared to its unmodified counterpart [
45
]. In addition to manual inspection of the MS/MS spectra, we took into consideration peptide retention times. For this, the extracted ion chromatogram (XIC) for each peptide identified showed a later elution time for citrullinated peptides compared with the unmodified version. Citrullination was only considered if it could be reliably distinguished from asparagine or glutamine deamidation, and if there was sufficient b- and y-fragment ion coverage surrounding the modified site.

Antigenic peptides were conjugated to KLH and/or OVA and sometimes a 50:50 conjugation mix depending on the antigen. Citrullinated tau antibodies were purified using affinity chromatography with modified versus unmodified peptides and quality control (Q/C) immunodepletion. Briefly, antibodies were purified using the peptide antigens bound to an iodoacetyl resin. Two milligrams of each antigen peptide were incubated for 1 h at room temperature in pH 7.4 phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Resins were then washed three times with PBS pH 7.4 and antibodies were eluted using 0.1 M glycine–HCl buffer, pH 3. Eluted antibodies were dialyzed against PBS, pH 7.4 and measured by absorbance at 280 nm to determine the antibody concentration. Antibodies that showed reactivity to non-modified tau were subjected to additional rounds of post-immuno-depletion using peptide affinity resins coupled to non-modified peptides. Brain cortical tissue was homogenized in detergent extraction buffer including RIPA (25 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 1% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS) with 1 mM PMSF, protease inhibitor cocktail, and phosphatase inhibitor cocktails II and III (Sigma Aldrich, MO, USA) and centrifuged at 14,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Gallyas staining was performed as described [

Briefly, slides were treated with 5% periodic acid (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) for 5 min, washed with water, and incubated sequentially for 1 min in silver iodide (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) and 10 min with 0.5% acetic acid (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) solutions prior to being placed in developer solution (2.5% sodium carbonate, 0.1% ammonium nitrate, 0.1% silver nitrate, 1% tungstosilicic acid, 0.7% formaldehyde) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA). Immuno-labeled sections were imaged using a Zeiss Axio Scan Z1 digital slide scanner at various magnifications as indicated in each figure legend. Introduction
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) comprises several hallmarks, one of which includes tau deposition. Decades of research show that aberrant tau biology elicits loss of tau function, transitions from soluble to insoluble tau aggregates and neurofibrillary tangles (NFT), neurodegeneration, and ultimately cognitive impairment. Electron cryo-microscopy (CryoEm) has uncovered the diversity of tau proteoforms for the evolving class of tauopathies. Increasing reports illustrate how tau dysfunction impacts critical physiological processes, including mitochondria bioenergetics and synaptic plasticity [
55
], and autophagy impairment [
11
,
14
,
15
], that subsequently lead to different clinical syndromes. There is an urgent need to understand how different variants, strains, and proteoforms of tau influence biology for anti-tau approaches.
The mammalian genome codes for only 20 natural amino acids, but the diversity of posttranslational modifications (PTMs) provides more flexibility in protein structure and function that can produce more than one hundred secondary (derived) amino acids [
57
], thus allowing unique and new features for a single protein. Tau protein is a substrate for several PTMs including hyperphosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, methylation, glycosylation, nitration, and others less well studied [
3
,
11
,
37
]. Phosphorylation is recognized as the most studied tau PTM and remains the best understood, where the hyperphosphorylation is thought to initiate the pathogenic sequelae of tau aggregation [
19
,
33
,
50
]. Recent studies using cryoEM technology have been instrumental in investigating the role of PTMs in promoting strain and conformation differences [
5
], signifying a need to understand other PTMs in tauopathies. Given the dynamic complexity of PTMs in tauopathies [
9
,
16
,
48
], it is plausible that less well-studied modifications add to tau diversity and contribute to subtypes of the clinical spectrum.
Citrullination (citR; also called deamination) is an irreversible PTM catalyzed by peptidyl arginine deiminases (PADs) that involves the conversion of the amino acid arginine to citrulline within proteins and peptides [
4
]. Citrullination yields the loss of a positive charge coupled with a 0.98 Da increase in mass [
46
], which increases the hydrophobicity of the structural moiety [
13
]. In addition, the neutralization of positively charged arginine residues significantly alters protein structure as well as stabilizes protein–protein, protein–DNA, and protein–RNA, interactions [
22
,
65
]. Peptidyl arginine deiminase (
PADI
) genes, encoding the 5 human PAD isoforms (PAD1–5), are located in a single gene cluster on chromosome 1p36.1 in humans and chromosome 4pE1 in mice [
60
,
61
]. Influx of, or increased, intracellular calcium activates PADs in a coordinated manner through five calcium binding sites (C1–C5) to form a catalytically competent active site [
6
,
35
,
46
]. Reports illustrate increased PAD4 expression throughout the cytoplasm of pyramidal neurons with age and in AD human brain [
26
,
61
]. In addition, previous studies demonstrated PAD2 and PAD4 co-localization with citrullinated proteins in the cortex and hippocampus of AD brain tissue [
2
,
26
]. Acharya and colleagues provided further evidence of the co-localization of pan-citrullinated proteins with amyloid beta and PAD4 in the cytoplasm of cortical pyramidal and hippocampal hilus neurons [
2
]. Finally, several citrullinated proteins were identified in various regions of AD brain tissue including GFAP, MBP, HSP90, ENO1, NSE, and PTCD2. In addition, amyloid beta can also become citrullinated during AD [
26
,
41
].
Herein, we show that full-length tau is a client of both PAD4 and PAD2, which can become fully citrullinated at all 14 arginine residues using recombinant protein systems. The development of a panel of highly specific citR tau antibodies further demonstrated the extent of tau citrullination in cellular and animal models of tauopathy as well as human AD brain tissue. In tauopathy mice with frontotemporal degeneration (FTD) mutations, PAD4 increased early during tau pathogenesis along with citR tau, which accumulated in soluble and detergent-soluble fractions. CitR tau was also increased in human AD tissue with a higher pathological tau burden. Overall, this study provides a necessary framework to understand the role of citrullination as a common PTM in AD.

Mass spectroscopy
Samples from enzyme reactions with tau protein incubated with PAD2 or PAD4 were separated by SDS-PAGE and Coomassie-stained for visualization. Bands were excised from the gel and processed for LC–MS/MS analysis. Briefly, each gel piece was minced and de-stained before being reduced with dithiothreitol (DTT), alkylated with iodoacetamide (IAA), and finally digested with Trypsin/Lys-C overnight at 37 °C. Peptides were extracted using 50/50 acetonitrile (ACN)/H
2
O/0.1% formic acid and dried in a vacuum concentrator. Peptides were resuspended in 98% H
2
O/2% ACN/0.1% formic acid for LC–MS/MS analysis.
Peptides were separated on a 50 cm C18 reversed-phase UHPLC column (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) using an Ultimate3000 UHPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) with a 60 min gradient (4–40% ACN/0.1% formic acid) and analyzed on a hybrid quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Q Exactive Plus, Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) using data-dependent acquisition in which the top 10 most abundant ions are selected for MS/MS analysis. Full MS survey scans were acquired at 70,000 resolution.
Raw data files were processed in MaxQuant (
www.maxquant.org
) and searched against the current Uniprot
Homo sapiens
protein sequence database. Search parameters included constant modification of cysteine by carbamidomethylation, and the variable modifications, methionine oxidation, arginine citrullination, as well as asparagine and glutamine deamidation. Proteins are identified using the filtering criteria of 1% protein and peptide false discovery rate, with a peptide tolerance of 4.5 ppm.
To ensure the correct identification of the site-specific citrullination of Tau411, several factors were taken into consideration. MS/MS spectra were manually annotated to verify the sequence coverage of each citrulline-containing peptide. The verification process further included consideration of deamidation of asparagine and glutamine, which results in an identical mass shift as the citrullination of arginine. While deamidation cannot be differentiated from citrullination based on mass, deamidation does not affect the charge of the amino acid residue (under acidic LC–MS conditions); however, citrulline neutralizes a positively charged arginine. The reduced positive charge/increased hydrophobicity of a peptide containing a citrullinated arginine results in a later elution time compared to its unmodified counterpart [
45
]. In addition to manual inspection of the MS/MS spectra, we took into consideration peptide retention times. For this, the extracted ion chromatogram (XIC) for each peptide identified showed a later elution time for citrullinated peptides compared with the unmodified version. Citrullination was only considered if it could be reliably distinguished from asparagine or glutamine deamidation, and if there was sufficient b- and y-fragment ion coverage surrounding the modified site.

Little is known about the functional state of citrullinated tau. Given the charge neutralization, increased hydrophobicity, and reduced π–π interactions, we sought to understand the effect of citrullination on the intrinsic disordered status of tau using bioinformatics tools. There are no natural codons that code for citrulline, and this residue, being not common or well characterized in protein structures, is not included in any computational analytic platforms. Therefore, to mimic the potential citrullination effects, we changed all arginine (R) residues to glutamine (Q) residues in the 2N4R tau as pseudomimetics for citrulline and used a set of computational tools designed for the intrinsic disorder analysis. This all R-to-Q substitution in tau caused a slight increase in the overall mean hydrophobicity (from 0.4036 to 0.4071 in Kate–Doolittle hydropathy scale of the protein [
30
]). At the same time, the total protein charge changed from + 2 to − 12, leading to an increase in the absolute mean net charge from 0.0045 to 0.0272. As a result, the position of a pseudo-citrullinated R → Q tau within the charge-hydropathy (CH) plot [
43
,
56
] shifted closer to the boundary separating disordered and ordered proteins (distance to the boundary decreased from 0.0273 to 0.0160, data not shown), indicating that citrullination might lead to a slight decrease in the overall disorder predisposition of tau. This is an interesting, conflicting, and not an obvious conclusion, since pseudo-citrullination shows opposite effects on tau hydrophobicity and mean net charge. According to the logic behind the CH-plot analysis, increased hydrophobicity should lead to a decrease in disorder propensity, whereas increased mean net charge is typically associated with an increase in disorder potential. This conclusion is further supported by the evaluation of the per-residue disorder propensity of tau and pseudo-citrullinated R → Q tau by a set of commonly used disorder predictors assembled using the RIDAO platform [
12
]. Results of these analyses are summarized in Fig.
2

The mean disorder characteristics (percent of predicted intrinsically disordered residues (PPIRD) and average disorder score (ADS)) generated by these tools provide further evidence of the “confusing” outputs of pseudo-citrullination. In fact, the normal tau is characterized by PPIDR-ADS of 65.99–0.6714 (PONDR

Since tau is known to undergo liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS), at the next step, we focused on how pseudo-citrullination might affect the LLPS potential of this protein. Results of the corresponding analysis by FuzDrop [

59
] are shown in Fig.

= 0.9963 versus 0.9951). Normal tau has two droplet-promoting regions (DPRs, residues 1–265 and 401–423), as well as four aggregation hot spots (residues 3–12, 224–229, 245–252, and 401–423), i.e., regions that might drive protein aggregation within the droplets. There are also 9 regions with context-dependent interactions or regions with multiplicity of binding modes (MBM, residues 3–12, 224–229, 245–252, 261–287, 293–306, 355–361, 366–374, 399–430, and 433–438), i.e., regions that exhibit different binding modes depending on the peculiarities of cellular context (sub-cellular localization, partners, posttranslational modifications, etc.). On the other hand, there are three DPRs (residues 1–273, 291–304, and 398–423) in the pseudo-citrullinated R → Q tau, which also contains 6 aggregation hot spots (residues 3–12, 110–117, 244–252, 268–273, 292–302, and 398–420) and 9 MBM regions (residues 3–12, 110–117, 244–252, 268–286, 292–302, 355–363, 366–374, 389–420, and 423–438). These results indicate that citrullination might affect the LLPS potential of tau and may enhance the aggregation predisposition of tau, since it results in the doubling of the number of aggregation hot spots.
Based on these outputs of the computational analyses, one might suggest that pseudo-citrullination increases the hydrophobicity of tau and renders this protein slightly more ordered and more prone to spontaneous LLPS. It also furnishes the protein with higher aggregation potential likely due to the increased potential to form oligomers due to the increased local hydrophobicity.

Calcium load and PAD4 expression regulate substrate specificity for citR tau epitopes
An important yet untested hypothesis for citrullination via PAD activity, and perhaps the most biologically intriguing mechanism, is that PAD4 displays different “
coordinated activation states
” depending on its five Ca
2+
-binding pockets. Low Ca
2+
load may display high substrate specificity (i.e., restricted epitope citrullination), whereas high Ca
2+
-binding capacity displays low substrate specificity (i.e., non-restricted citrullination). An alternative to non-restricted citrullination may also depend on PAD concentration itself. If true, this would suggest that certain regions within tau may undergo citrullination at different rates depending on calcium loads, PAD concentration and pathological stages (aberrant Ca
2+
dysfunction) of disease. Given our panel of citrullinated tau antibodies and the ability to measure tau at multiple functional domains, we sought to test this by monitoring the degree of tau citrullination at six citR tau sites (i.e., tau citR170, citR 194, citR 209, citR230, citR349, and citR406) under various PAD4 concentrations (0.67–670 nM) with high calcium load (10 mM) or without calcium (Fig.
4
a, b). Indeed, PAD4 concentration (670 nM) with high calcium load (10 mM) citrullinated all six tau sites tested. Interestingly PAD4 (670 nM) with no calcium also citrullinated tau at citR194, citR209, citR230, and citR349 equally; however, citrullination of citR170 and tau citR406 was diminished when calcium was absent suggesting that certain citR epitopes are sensitive to coordinated calcium activation of PAD4. Importantly, a tenfold lower concentration of PAD4 (67 nM) with high calcium load (10 mM) was also able to restore citrullination of tau citR170 and tau citR406 beyond that of PAD4 (670 nM + 0 mM calcium) also indicating the degree of PAD4 specificity for selective epitopes. As PAD4 concentration decreased, citrullination of tau also decreased at all epitopes. These data suggest that citrullination of tau depends on both PAD4 concentration and calcium load but can vary in epitope specificity depending on the coordinated state of calcium activation of PAD4. This is a notable finding for an irreversible modification because it dictates how a limited number of PADs expressed in the brain potentially regulate many proteins with substrate specificity.

Discussion
In the current study, we identified citrullination of tau on multiple epitopes using the 2N4R (441a.a) isoform under several conditions including recombinant protein reactions, cellular models, animal models of tau deposition, and human tissue. Given that several reports demonstrated increased PAD2/PAD4 activity and hypercitrullination in Alzheimer’s disease brain [
26
], we primarily focused our study on these two isoforms. However, it is unclear if other PADs (PAD1, PAD3, PAD5) have been identified in the mammalian brain or if they express at lower levels than PAD2/PAD4. We confirmed increased PAD2 and PAD4 in a small cohort of AD and control samples, but identified higher expression in AD brains with higher phospho-tau burden. Although PAD2 and PAD4 protein expression increased in AD, protein abundance may not be a rate-limiting step to increase citrullination activity. PADs compete with and are coordinately activated with calcium load; therefore, aberrant calcium dysfunction, observed in AD could produce regional or cell-specific hypercitrullination and thereby hyper-citrullinated tau. It is also not clear as to the timing of citR tau in AD samples as being early, late or parallel in staging to phosphorylation, which could potentially shape the tau landscape and consideration of anti-tau approaches.
We demonstrated that tau was susceptible to becoming fully citrullinated using recombinant protein systems and that this depended on PAD concentration, calcium load, and substrate selectivity; however, it remains unclear if all tau isoforms or strains are citrullinated to the same extent in vivo. Given that citrullination is putatively irreversible, future work is necessary to uncover how it impacts tau’s physiologic function including microtubule biology, turnover rate, and aggregation profile. We simulated pseudo-citrullination on tau with arginine to glutamine residues to begin to understand the disorder ranking of the modification. The converted modification was not an obvious conclusion based on changes in the charge neutralization, increased hydrophobicity, and reduced pi–pi bond interactions. Increased hydrophobicity should typically decrease disorder potential, whereas increased mean net charge, which is the case for tau citrullination associates with increased disorder propensity. Computational analysis suggests that because of the increased local hydrophobicity, citrullinated tau might be slightly more ordered, form spontaneous LLPS, and possibly be prone to more aggregates under these conditions due to the increased potential to form oligomers. This possibility warrants further experimental testing to understand the full extent and dynamic interactions of citrullinated tau’s biophysical properties in the context of spontaneous LLPS versus fibrillization (beta sheet formation). We showed that citrullinated tau or pseudo-citrullinated (R → Q) tau generally delayed ThioT incorporation/fibrillization under various conditions including both wild-type and P301L tau. Our data indicate that as tau became more fully citrullinated, the fibrillization rate slowed and Vmax was reduced; but when tau was partially citrullinated, the aggregation rate still slowed but Vmax still increased. Although these data may not be completely generalizable, these conditions suggest that citrullination of tau may extend the oligomeric phase. However if true, citR tau could potentially delay tau positron emission tomography (PET) positivity detection in patients. Structurally, it is unclear during this slow progression phase if different polymorphs or various tau proteoforms emerge. We identified neurons that harbor only citR tau or phospho-tau, but also some neurons that label both. This is an important consideration because tau pathology is predominantly defined by its phosphorylation status and remains the focus of therapeutic interventions. It is plausible that citR tau pathology can emerge independently, in parallel, but also converge with phospho-tau pathology during staging. Future studies will be important to understand the degree of both citR tau and phospho-tau on the same molecule and if citrullination impacts phosphorylation state and vice versa.
A recent study showed that arginine pi–pi bonds within tau were key determinants for tau’s protein network and demonstrated how arginine residues drive aberrant interactions of proteins with tau fibrils [
18
]. The higher order aggregation from monomer to fibril formation rewired avidity properties of tau and attracted new sets of interactor proteins for the tau proteome. Tau’s proline-rich region and projection domain perhaps drive many of these interactions. Structurally, another report [
34
] demonstrated that pseudo-phosphorylation mimics of tau at 12 selective epitopes were able to recapitulate the ordered core of the Alzheimer’s disease tau fold and that many of these pseudo-phospho sites fell outside the ordered core but within the fuzzy coat. Most notably, several pseudo-phosphomimics were located within the proline-rich region including ptau (T181, S202, T205, T212, S214, T217, T231 and S235), indicating that domains outside the ordered core heavily influence tau folds. Interestingly, the highest stretch of tau citrullination occurs within the proline-rich region, and therefore, it is tempting to speculate if citrullination impacts tau folds or directs polymorphs. This domain may serve as a scaffold and signaling hub as previously suggested [
40
]. In general, citrullination endorses protein unfolding, increases hydrophobicity, reduces the overall net charge, causes a loss of ionic bonds, and interferes with H-bond stabilization [
53
]. Collectively, these features create difficulty in predicting how citrullination could influence tau or other disordered protein’s final permutation in disease. However, our current work offers an alternative interpretation for the tau spectrum.

Nevertheless, glial PAD2 expression does not preclude its low neuronal expression and given the stepwise calcium activation of PAD2, one cannot rule out the effect of citrullinated tau from PAD2 or possibly other PADs with low neuronal expression. Various forms of tau are unique in that soluble aggregates, insoluble aggregates, different proteoforms and tangles all associate with some measure of toxicity but manifest diverse clinical syndromes, variable phenotypes, and regionally accumulate in different areas of the brain. Increasing evidence suggests that tau can form soluble aggregates versus fibrillar aggregates and that these may emerge from soluble unfolded oligomers versus folded or fibrillar oligomers; however, it is unclear which species is more toxic. The collective behavior of citrullinated tau would speculate that it favors unfolded oligomers, soluble aggregates, and the “off pathway” to fibril assembly; however, more work is needed to test this. A recent study demonstrated in mice that non-tangle bearing neurons died more frequently and were at risk of cell death compared to neurons containing fibrillar tau aggregates. Similar microstructural alterations were also identified in human AD brains fueling the ongoing debate of the tau spectrum in isolating toxic tau strains and proteoforms [
20
]. It is also plausible that irreversible citrullination locks tau into specific proteoforms.
Although several of the citrullinated tau epitopes were not yet tested or shown for AD in the current study (i.e., tau citR170, tau citR194, tau citR209, tau citR231, and tau citR349 shown), ten antibodies labeled citR tau in animal models of tau deposition (shown: tau citR170, tau citR194, tau citR209, tau citR231, and tau citR349; not shown: tau citR5, tau citR23, tau citR155, tau citR221, tau citR379, tau citR406). One goal of this study was to create and characterize a panel of citrullinated tau antibodies to test future hypotheses for domain-specific functions of tau but to also demonstrate how promiscuous PAD’s are at citrullinating a single protein. It is important to highlight one critical finding in our dataset, which showed that citrullination of tau-obscured recognition of Tau5 antibody binding (Fig.
3
b, and Supplemental Figure 2b). This finding is highly intriguing because only three arginine residues remain susceptible to citrullination (tau citR211, tau citR221, and citR230, whereas tau citR209 and tau citR242 are flanking) within the Tau5 antibody epitope sequence (210–241); yet, this combination significantly reduced Tau5 antibody immunoreactivity. This phenomenon has several potential implications: 1) it suggests that citrullination may significantly alter tau’s protein structure in this region; 2) the structural changes within the proline-rich region from citrullination could potentially impact the Alzheimer’s disease tau fold (i.e., T181, S202, T205, T212, S214, T217, T231 and S235); 3) citR tau could possibly evade antibody biomarker detection and diagnosis particularly for markers within the proline-rich region (i.e., S212, S214, T217, T231); and 4) citrullination could reduce tau immunotherapy depending on epitope-targeting domains. Several clinical trial immunotherapies to tau (ongoing, recruiting, or completed) target sites that contain citrullination-susceptible regions. Five tau immunotherapies contain citrullinated tau epitopes within the antigenic sequence, while another five contain citR tau sites at − 2, − 1, + 1, and + 2 immediately flanking the immunotherapy antigenic sequence [
67
]. Therefore, further work is essential to understand if citrullinated tau plays a role in immunotherapy efficacy and how to interpret clinical trial outcomes regarding epitope sequences for anti-tau approaches.
Another question we sought to answer is how calcium load impacts PAD4’s substrate specificity on various tau epitopes. We found that higher concentrations of PAD4 (> 500 nM) citrullinated several arginine’s on tau even in the absence of calcium, whereas low concentrations of PAD4 (approximately 10–100-fold less) citrullinated specific arginine residues on tau only in the presence of high calcium (10 mM). These data suggest that low abundance PAD4 expression coupled with high or aberrant calcium load modifies the specificity of citrullinated substrates on tau. It also suggests that increased expression of PAD4 potentially with or without calcium causes low substrate specificity possibly leading to hypercitrullination of tau. Importantly, calcium induces the activity of PAD4 by a factor of 100,000 and PAD2 greater than 700,000 [
6
,
10
,
51
]. Given the sensitivity of calcium load and the limited number of PADs expressed in neurons versus glia, citR tau potentially reflects an alternative type of tau pathology that could be directly related to calcium dysfunction. Our data indicate that selective tau epitopes are more sensitive to calcium load with lower PAD concentrations than others and could potentially be exploited as biomarkers for early calcium-induced citR tau providing an alternative arm of the tau spectrum in AD. Notably, these conclusions are in context with recombinant protein systems under optimal buffer conditions. However, our data also provide some perspective as to the versatility of PAD-induced citrullination and depend on calcium load, PAD levels, and the substrate/epitope client itself. From a therapeutic angle, the potency and efficacy of PAD inhibitors will need to be tailored to disease conditions based on these considerations. Recent development of PAD inhibitors has demonstrated hyper citrullination as a therapeutic target in animal models of ischemic stroke [
29
], multiple sclerosis [
38
,
54
], TBI [
58
], spinal cord injury [
17
], and neonatal hypoxic ischemia [
31
]. Here, we also validated that high concentrations of the PAD inhibitor BB-CL-amidine prevented citrullination of recombinant tau and slowed aggregation rate during a ThioT assay, suggesting its utility as a potential therapeutic approach in AD. Although we do not yet know how citrullinated tau impacts neuronal toxicity, future studies will be important to test PAD inhibitors and knockout studies in models of tau deposition.
In conclusion, we identified that tau is susceptible to becoming fully citrullinated at all 14 arginine residues through PAD4 and PAD2 and that novel antibodies to citR tau detect pathology in animal models with tau deposition and during AD neuropathologic change. Future studies will be important to understand the full extent of tau citrullination and the functional impact on disease outcomes. Identifying the regulatory mechanisms of PADs during AD pathogenesis may also serve as a therapeutic node to different stages of tau progression and even biomarkers [
49
]. Together, this work provides an alternative area of tau biology that warrants further understanding and consideration as a potential target for anti-tau approaches.
